Testing the CVaR Model Against a Known Answer

Testing the CVaR Model Against a Known Answer

Monte Carlo study on synthetic data, then validation on a trend-following backtest rebuilt from public prices.

Nate Kaul · AlgoGators Quant Trading · October 2026

What this covers

The problem it set out to solve: on real data you never know the right answer. If a model's 99% estimate gets breached on 2% of days, that could mean the model understates risk by half, or it could mean the sample was unlucky — and nothing in the data separates the two. So the model was tested somewhere the answer is known, and then the predictions that test produced were checked against real data.

Along the way the second problem became unavoidable: the backtest database cannot support a coverage test, so a clean one was rebuilt from public futures prices. That rebuild is the first time this model has been scored on a genuinely long/short book.

The three findings

1. Any estimator that reads its quantile off a normal distribution has a fixed tail shape.

The ratio of its 99% number to its 90% number is locked at 1.82 — a property of the formula, not of the data. On processes carrying this strategy's measured parameters the true ratio is 2.18. That 17% shortfall produces a specific signature: comfortable at the 90% level, breaking through at the 99%. Only two of six estimators get the shape right.

2. On a clean long/short book, both our models over-breach at every level.

Roughly double the expected rate at 99%, for both the original model and its replacement, over 7,305 test days. The cause is not tail shape — that is within 5% — but scale: the models are about 25% too narrow, persistently.

3. A trailing scale correction fixes it, and it holds on data it never saw.

One parameter, selected on a training half, validated on a held-out half. The pre-registered choice gets the body right and the tail marginally wrong; slightly longer windows pass at all three levels.

The shortfall is a portfolio-level effect. Each market's own volatility is already filtered by its own GARCH, so what is missing is how much the markets move together — which is exactly what a trend book is concentrated in, because the rules put on correlated bets by construction.

What this forces us to decide

# Decision What the evidence says
1 Adopt the scale correction? The model is 25% too narrow on clean data. The correction is one trailing parameter and survives out-of-sample validation. Recommend adopting, with a 1,000-day window.
2 Keep or retire the correlation regime? The plan of record requires a regime-switching correlation state. Measured dependence in this book does not exceed an elliptical null, so a regime is not the right shape. But the portfolio-level effect the regime was meant to capture is real and is what finding 2 identifies. Recommend: satisfy the requirement with the scale layer, not a regime, and record it as a deviation.
3 Drop the annual CVaR figure? It cannot be validated and will not be. Recommend dropping it rather than reporting an unvalidated number.
4 Accept public-price validation as standing practice? The backtest database leaves 18 of 549 runs usable and one holding shorts. Public prices give 8,565 clean days with 37.5% short exposure. Recommend adopting as the standing validation substrate until the database is fixed.

Part I — Synthetic data, where the answer is known

The design

Four process families, each standardised to unit unconditional variance, so differences between them are differences of shape and never of scale:

family what it isolates
normal the control — no fat tails, no skew, no clustering
Student-t tail thickness alone, indexed by tail index ν
Hansen skewed-t asymmetry, with the left tail fattened independently
GARCH(1,1) volatility clustering, persistence α+β on a dial

Six estimators are scored against every cell — naive historical, a 4-sigma rule, a moving average, EWMA, GARCH-normal, GARCH-t — across four estimation windows and three confidence levels.

Indexed by tail index, not kurtosis. Our measured per-market tail indices run from 2.7 to 18.9, and kurtosis does not exist below ν = 4. Indexing by kurtosis would have silently dropped the regime where naive methods fail hardest.

Ground truth is the entire point of the exercise, so none of it is taken on faith.

Finding 1 in detail: the tail-shape ceiling

The ratio of an estimator's 99% number to its 90% number is a scale-free measure of tail curvature. For anything reading its quantile off a normal distribution:

Φ−1(0.99)Φ−1(0.90)=2.3261.282=1.82\frac{\Phi^{-1}(0.99)}{\Phi^{-1}(0.90)} = \frac{2.326}{1.282} = 1.82

No amount of data moves it. On a process carrying our measured parameters — tail index 6.9, skewness −0.21, persistence 0.984 — the truth is 2.18.

estimator shape ratio verdict
moving average, EWMA, GARCH-normal 1.82 at every window flat by 17%
GARCH-t 2.08 – 2.11 close
naive historical 2.29 – 2.48 slightly over-steep

This is why it matters operationally: an estimator whose tail is too flat is generous in the body and short in the extreme. It under-breaches at 90% and over-breaches at 99%. That pattern is recognisable in real coverage output, and it tells you the problem is shape rather than level.

Fat tails: a normal quantile understates VaR, and the gap widens as the tail thickens

The operational consequence — how often losses break through the estimate

Where each method breaks

The output is deliberately not a ranking. Different methods fail in different places, and a ranking would hide exactly that.

question answer from the grid
When does a reactive volatility model beat a flat window? Only once persistence exceeds ~0.9. Below that the flat window wins on RMSE.
When does assuming a normal tail stop being acceptable? Below tail index ≈ 8 the 99% breach rate passes 1.25%; below 5 it fails outright.
How much history before the empirical method overtakes the parametric one? Around 1,000 days. Below that GARCH-t wins; above it naive historical does.
What does over-fitting cost? GARCH-t on data with no fat tails and no clustering carries a 30–70% RMSE penalty versus a moving average.
What does skewness do? Every symmetric method fails. At λ = −0.6, GARCH-t is 21% low and a moving average 27% low. Naive historical is within 4%, because it never assumed symmetry.

Clustering: where a reactive volatility model earns its keep

Skewness: every symmetric method fails; the empirical one does not

Part II — A backtest worth testing against

Why we could not use our own

The coverage test needs a backtest to score against. Ours is a collection of unverified runs of mixed provenance. A quality screen — flat account-value histories, inconsistent position-to-equity dating, blended strategies with nothing in the schema to flag them — left 18 of 549 runs usable, and exactly one holding short positions, with 27 position records.

A trend-following strategy is long/short by definition. Validating its risk model on an effectively long-only sample tests something other than the strategy.

What we used instead

Prices from pysystemtrade, Rob Carver's public repository — the same author as the book our rules follow. 34 of our 36 markets are present (Brazilian real and Kansas wheat are not). Daily closes resampled from intraday bars give 8,565 trading days, 1990 to 2024.

The rule is our own reimplemented EWMAC: three speed pairs, Carver's forecast scalars, ±20 caps, FDM 1.45, 20% volatility target, 10% position buffer, and an instrument diversification multiplier re-estimated quarterly on trailing data.

One technical point worth making to anyone who asks about contract specs. Back-adjusted futures prices can cross zero, so this works in price differences normalised by a volatility in the same units. With

contractsi=fi10⋅C⋅τNσi,P&Li=contractsi⋅Δpi\text{contracts}_i = \frac{f_i}{10}\cdot\frac{C\cdot\tau}{N\,\sigma_i}, \qquad \text{P\&L}_i = \text{contracts}_i \cdot \Delta p_i

the price units cancel exactly — contract multipliers and quote currencies drop out of the risk-targeted P&L. Their absence cannot bias this backtest.

  Sharpe (excess=0)         0.77

The rebuilt backtest, 1990–2024

Is it credible? Four checks, not decorations

  • Monthly skewness +1.04. Positive skew is trend following's structural signature — many small losses, occasional large gains. A backtest without it is not trend following.
  • Sharpe by decade 0.83 / 1.01 / 0.30 / 1.00. The 2010s trough and 2020s recovery match the documented industry pattern. A backtest that performed uniformly well would be the suspicious one.
  • 37.5% of market-days short. Genuinely two-sided — the property our own data could not give.
  • Max drawdown −33.5% against a published 12-market replication's −30%, with a higher Sharpe consistent with 34 markets rather than 12.

Gross of transaction costs, which inflates the Sharpe ratio. It does not materially affect the tail behaviour under test.

Part III — The coverage test

Two models, scored walk-forward on identical days with identical positions:

  • OLD — multivariate Student-t on an EWMA covariance matrix, one shared tail parameter for all markets, no mechanism for volatility clustering.
  • NEW — filtered historical simulation: per-market GARCH(1,1) for conditional volatility, then whole-day vectors of standardised residuals resampled from the trailing pool, so each market keeps its own tail shape and cross-market structure survives without a correlation model.

Parameters refitted annually on trailing data; between refits the volatility recursion runs forward on realised returns, which is a one-step-ahead filter rather than a smoother. The residual pool at date t contains only residuals dated before t.

A bug found before the result

The backtest's trading index has gaps, so recovering "yesterday's position" by shifting one row picks a non-adjacent day wherever a gap falls — 95 of 8,564 rows. Fixed by lagging the position and volatility panels before filtering and saving them that way, so nothing downstream re-derives them. The test now carries an identity check: exposure times market moves must reproduce the realised loss. It does, to 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁴.

The fix moved the 99% breach rate from 2.55% to 2.49% — which is the only reason the failure below is worth reporting. It is the model's, not the plumbing's.

Both fail — and tail shape is not why

Look at the shape row. The NEW model's conditional tail shape is 2.10 against a realised 2.18 — about 5% flat, which is the magnitude Part I predicted for a filtered-historical method. Shape is close to right. Something else is wrong.

Two measurements that would have misled us, named here because both are easy to reach for:

  1. Backing a portfolio σ out of the model's own 90% quantile as VaR₉₀ / 1.2816. The FHS distribution is fat-tailed, so its 90% quantile is not 1.2816σ. Dividing by 1.2816 understates σ and manufactures a scale shortfall that is an artefact of assuming normality. This produced an apparent 29% gap that does not exist.
  2. Comparing the pooled realised quantile against the mean predicted quantile. Pooling realised losses across days of different volatility mixes an unconditional object with a conditional one. On a synthetic process where both are known exactly, the pooled ratio is 2.55 against a conditional 2.18 — a 1.17× spread present by construction, with the model exactly right. The real data shows 1.22×. A comparison that ignores this reports a 46% tail deficit where there is none.

What is used instead: breach rates, which are conditional by construction; the scale-free ratio loss / VaR₉₀ for timing only; and a same-day comparison of the model's scale against a trailing realised covariance on identical exposures, which compares two conditional objects.

The diagnosis

The miss is scale, and it is persistent rather than timed. The autocorrelation of |loss / VaR₉₀| is +0.046 at lag 1 — almost no dynamic structure is left for a smarter volatility model to capture. Meanwhile the same-day exposures run through a trailing realised covariance give 8–11% more risk than the model's own number, almost all of the time.

Since each market's own volatility is already filtered by its own GARCH, what is missing is a portfolio-level quantity: how much the markets move together. A trend book is concentrated in exactly that — long the whole bond complex, or short the whole dollar bloc, at once — so the portfolio is less diversified than per-market risk accounting implies.

This is the mechanism the plan of record calls correlation convergence. It is real. It is just not shaped like a regime switch.

Part IV — The correction, chosen blind

Why the split comes first

The obvious way to pick a correction is to try several and keep whichever gives the best full-sample coverage. That is selection on the test set. With a handful of candidates and three confidence levels, there is enough freedom to land near target by luck alone, and the result would mean nothing.

So the sample splits at 2010-01-01. Every choice — the form of the correction and its window — is made on the training half. The number reported is the held-out half.

Two candidates, both strictly trailing:

  • constant — one number k, the 90th percentile of loss / VaR₉₀ on the training half, then frozen. No adaptation at all. This is the baseline the adaptive version must beat.
  • trailing — k re-estimated daily as the 90th percentile of loss / VaR₉₀ over a trailing window.

Coverage on the held-out half, before and after correction

Reading this honestly

The model's VaR is 25% too small. That is the headline, estimated on training data alone.

The pre-registered choice — 500 days — gets the body right and the tail marginally wrong out of sample: 10.34% and 5.35% against targets of 10% and 5%, but 1.37% against 1%, which Kupiec rejects at p = 0.033. That is the primary result, because it is what the selection procedure actually chose.

Longer windows do better. A 1,000-day window gives 9.99 / 5.02 / 1.29 and passes at all three levels; 2,000 days also passes. Note the direction: the training half selected a window that is not the best out-of-sample performer. The selection worked against the reported result rather than flattering it, which is the right direction for that kind of error to run.

The constant baseline is informative in its failure. Frozen at ×1.253 it passes at 99% (p = 0.680) but becomes too conservative in the body — 8.26% and 3.98%. So adaptivity buys something: the trailing version holds all three levels where the constant holds one. The gap is modest, and longer windows converge toward the constant, consistent with the shortfall being a stable feature rather than a moving one.

Recommendation: adopt the 1,000-day trailing window, and report the 500-day result alongside it so the selection history is visible.

The same result through time — rolling 500-day breach rate at the 99% level

Does the synthetic half predict the real half?

This is the test that decides whether Part I was worth doing. Take the parameters measured on real filtered residuals — tail index 6.9, skewness −0.21, persistence 0.984 — find the matching cell in the synthetic grid, and read off what the study says coverage should be.

The conditional-versus-pooled spread that Part III depends on transfers almost exactly:

conditional pooled spread
synthetic process, both known exactly 2.18 2.55 1.17×
real data, 1,972 matched observations 2.20 2.54 1.22×

The synthetic study predicts the real data's behaviour to within a few percent on the quantity that matters. Its other conclusions can be relied on.

Limitations

Stated at the level a reviewer will press on.

The strategy is a reimplementation, not the production signal. The rule follows the published book our strategy is based on and correlates 0.964 with observed production signals, but it is not the same code. Conclusions about estimator behaviour transfer; exact risk numbers for the live book do not.

No transaction costs, so the backtest's Sharpe is optimistic. Tail behaviour under test is unaffected.

Two markets missing of 36, and the market set drifts — 24 live at the start of the test period, 34 at the end.

One split, not many. The held-out half is a single contiguous period, 2010–2024, and the 2010s were an unusual decade for this strategy. Rolling-origin validation would be stronger.

Only the one-day horizon is tested here. The coverage test scores a one-day horizon, where the book does not re-trade, so nothing in this study exercises the engine's path-dependent position simulation or speaks to whipsaw. That is a property of this test, not a missing piece of the engine — the engine does re-run the trend rule along each simulated path.

Monthly and annual horizons cannot be validated with available data. 167 independent monthly observations give a 99% test no power: it would accept any true breach rate between 0% and 2.4%.

What follows

Immediately actionable

  1. Wire the filtered-historical generator into the multi-day path loop. It currently feeds only the one-day path; the multi-day loop still draws from the older distribution. Contained change.
  2. Add the scale correction as a parameter on the engine's output.
  3. Make the 99/90 shape ratio a standing diagnostic. It is scale-free, separates shape error from level error, and instantly identifies any estimator reading its quantile off a normal.

Needs a decision — the five items in the table near the top.

Blocked on the database — validation against our own strategy's realised P&L, which is the only thing that can confirm these numbers for the live book rather than for a faithful reimplementation of it.
